claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a hierarchical heterostructure characterized by multilevel chemical fluctuations.

Combining phase-field-derived microstructural descriptors with physics-informed Gaussian Process Regression enables rapid and quantitatively accurate prediction of Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness.
Phase-field simulations of representative volume elements can provide descriptors of chemical fluctuations and local stiffness variations under tensile and fracture loading.
A limited set of targeted tensile and fracture measurements is sufficient to calibrate the proposed Gaussian Process Regression model.
Predictions are intended for room-temperature, moderate-strain-rate uniaxial tensile and fracture tests.
Reliable predictions require phase-field simulations that reproduce the experimentally observed representative microstructural environment.
Multilevel chemical fluctuations and local phase-boundary evolution modulate local stress propagation and dislocation behavior.
Phase-field-derived descriptors can encapsulate complex microstructure–property relationships and thereby reduce reliance on full-scale first-principles calculations.
Physics-based constraints allow the Gaussian Process Regression model to account for elastic and fracture mechanisms when predicting macroscopic properties.
The proposed method will predict Young’s modulus with an error of approximately 5% or less.
The proposed method will predict yield strength with an error of approximately 10% or less.
The proposed method will provide the first quantitative fracture-toughness estimates for this material.
The proposed method will reduce computational cost by a factor of 50–100 relative to full-scale simulations.
Direct first-principles prediction of alloy fracture or yield strength is computationally challenging and generally beyond available DFT implementations.
Traditional ab initio and molecular-dynamics methods have limitations in predicting fracture toughness and representing complex heterostructural features.
Model reliability may diminish at high temperatures, extreme strain rates, or during phase transitions absent from the simulation descriptors.
Failure of the phase-field simulation to capture critical microstructural phenomena may degrade predictions.
The surrogate model may be sensitive to errors in extracted microstructural descriptors and should be used cautiously outside its calibration range.
A blinded prospective benchmark will generate predictions before measuring Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture toughness on newly synthesized specimens.
The hypothesis is to be falsified if Young’s-modulus error exceeds 10%, yield-strength error exceeds 15%, or predicted fracture toughness fails to correlate with experimental trends.
